statement.p:
We will investigate the connection between the determinant of a matrix and its invertibility using Gaussian elimination.
Consider the two upper triangular matrices
U_1 = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ 0 \amp 2 \amp 4 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp -2 \\ \end{array}\right],~~~ U_2 = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ 0 \amp 2 \amp 4 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ \end{array}\right].
Which of the matrices U_1 and U_2 are invertible? What are the determinants \det(U_1) and \det(U_2)?
Explain why an upper triangular matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is not zero.
Let's now consider the matrix
A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ -2 \amp 2 \amp -6 \\ 3 \amp -1 \amp 10 \\ \end{array}\right] and begin the Gaussian elimination process with a row replacement operation
A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ -2 \amp 2 \amp -6 \\ 3 \amp -1 \amp 10 \\ \end{array}\right] \sim \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp -2 \\ 3 \amp -1 \amp 10 \\ \end{array}\right] = A_1 . What is the relationship between \det(A) and \det(A_1)?
Next we perform another row replacement operation:
A_1= \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp -2 \\ 3 \amp -1 \amp 10 \\ \end{array}\right] \sim \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp -2 \\ 0 \amp 2 \amp 4 \\ \end{array}\right] = A_2 . What is the relationship between \det(A) and \det(A_2)?
Finally, we perform an interchange:
A_2 = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp -2 \\ 0 \amp 2 \amp 4 \\ \end{array}\right] \sim \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp -1 \amp 2 \\ 0 \amp 2 \amp 4 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp -2 \\ \end{array}\right] = U
to arrive at an upper triangular matrix U. What is the relationship between \det(A) and \det(U)?
Since U is upper triangular, we can compute its determinant, which allows us to find \det(A). What is \det(A)? Is A invertible?
Now consider the matrix
A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp -1 \amp 3 \\ 0 \amp 2 \amp -2 \\ 2 \amp 1 \amp 3 \\ \end{array}\right].
Perform a sequence of row operations to find an upper triangular matrix U that is row equivalent to A. Use this to determine \det(A) and whether A is invertible.
Suppose we apply a sequence of row operations on a matrix A to obtain A'. Explain why \det(A) \neq 0 if and only if \det(A') \neq 0.
Explain why an n\times n matrix A is invertible if and only if \det(A) \neq 0.

li.p: The matrix U_1 is invertible because we see there is a pivot position in every row and column. The matrix U_2, however, is not invertible because there is not a pivot position in the third row. Also, \det(U_1)=-4 and \det(U_2)=0.

The determinant of an upper triangular matrix equals the product of its diagonal entries. Consequently, if the determinant of an upper triangular matrix is not zero, then each of its diagonal entries must be nonzero. In this case, there is a pivot position in every row and every column so that the matrix is invertible.
Row replacement operations do not change the determinant so \det(A) = \det(A_1).
Interchanges change the sign of the determinant so \det(A) = -\det(U).

The determinant \det(U) = -4 since it is the product of the diagonal entries of U. This means that \det(A) = 4. We see that A is invertible because U, which has a pivot position in every row and every column, is invertible.

Beginning with a row replacement operation, we arrive at A_1=\left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp - 1 \amp 3 \\ 0 \amp 2 \amp -2 \\ 0 \amp -3 \amp 3 \\ \end{array}\right]. We next scale the second row by \frac12 to obtain A_2=\left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp - 1 \amp 3 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp -1 \\ 0 \amp -3 \amp 3 \\ \end{array}\right]. Another row replacement operation gives A_3=\left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp - 1 \amp 3 \\ 0 \amp 1 \amp -1 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ \end{array}\right]. Putting these operations together, we see that \det(A) = 2\det(U) = 0. In this case, A is not invertible because U, which has a row without a pivot position, is not invertible.

Performing one of the three row operations either leaves the determinant unchanged (row replacement), changes its sign (interchange), or multiplies it by a nonzero number (scaling). Therefore, if we begin with a matrix whose determinant is not zero, the determinant remains nonzero after any row operation is applied.

If we apply a sequence of row operations to A to find a row equivalent matrix U that is upper triangular, we know that \det(A)
eq0 if and only if \det(U) 
eq 0. We also know that A is invertible if and only if U is invertible. Putting these facts together, we conclude that \det(A)
eq 0 if and only if A is invertible.
